title: Elite Universities Are a Cartel: They Sell Status, Not Education
dek: America's elite universities are not charitable educational institutions but a cartel that maintains its brand by freezing enrollment, running alumni donations, and absorbing federal research grants; they sell status, not education.
why: It dissects elite university finances through an RTS-game framework, wiring endowments, admissions, tenure, and federal grants into a single closed loop — a novel and counterintuitive angle.
who: Students and parents preparing to apply to US colleges, education entrepreneurs, investors watching the US innovation system and university finances, and anyone who wants to understand why elite universities keep getting more expensive.

points.h: High selectivity is not an educational advantage, it's a status business
points.body: The logic of the American-style free market is that privatization brings competition, competition produces meritocracy, and meritocracy drives innovation and lower prices. Universities are the counterexample: they were never treated as a market, yet they push prices to the highest in the world. Harvard, Stanford, Princeton, and MIT charge six figures a year, applications explode while enrollment slots have been frozen for decades, deliberately manufacturing scarcity just like Hermès and Ferrari. The host admits from his own workplace experience: Ivy League graduates are not smarter, and often talk more than they do; these schools have never produced data proving better teaching or better employment outcomes, so high selectivity has no educational basis — it's just a status business.

points.h: Alumni aren't a community, they're the school's sales pipeline
points.body: The advancement office is a sales organization wearing campus-spirit clothing, and its goal is to extract as much new money as possible. Every graduate is a potential harvest, and the wealthier you are, the more closely you're tracked. Alumni reunions, dinners, and annual giving campaigns are essentially free parties that let the school record your career, financial status, and probability of donating — no different from a sales team managing leads in Salesforce. Princeton alumni volunteers solicit classmates for free, giving it the highest donation participation rate in the country; the Harvard Red Book is a database of alumni self-reported income and occupation. Schools even hire people full-time to watch for liquidity events like IPOs, company sales, and inheritances, because those are the best moments to harvest.

points.h: Money lost on teams and dorms is a donation decades later
points.body: Elite universities manufacture membership identity through layer upon layer of small groups: Yale's 14 residential colleges, Harvard's 12 houses, Princeton's 11 eating clubs, stacked with fraternities, sororities, and societies. Over 90% of Harvard and Princeton undergraduates live on campus for four years, and there is one varsity team for every 150 students; the Ivy League bans athletic scholarships, sports programs run at a total loss, and their only job is to manufacture spiritual stickiness. These facilities are like the "happiness buildings" in an RTS: not cheap, and their purpose is to bind students' formative years from 18 to 22 to their alma mater in exchange for donations decades later. Dorms, dining halls, and gyms are all loss-making investments, but only elite schools can afford them, because they have few students and concentrated investment.

points.h: In the longest bull market ever, endowments lost to an index fund
points.body: The endowment office's only task is to make the money bigger; its fund managers are the highest paid in the whole school, often poached from Wall Street, investing in private equity and venture capital chasing unicorns. About 5% of the endowment's value is drawn each year for operations, spent on schedule regardless of whether markets rise or fall, to smooth out bad years. But the biggest irony is this: even in the longest bull market in history, after fees almost every school underperformed an ordinary Vanguard index fund, and Harvard lost the most. Because undergraduate enrollment is frozen, tuition is loss-leading customer acquisition, and the endowment covers about two-thirds of these universities' annual operating budgets. And most of the money in the endowment is restricted; only small annual gifts are unrestricted, which is why schools still desperately maintain alumni relations.

points.h: When the provost moves one faculty slot, he sentences a department to death
points.body: The person actually running the university is the provost, who decides each department's budget and staffing. The strongest unit is the professor: after a six-year term comes the tenure review, and once passed, the school pays a salary forever and can hardly ever fire them; the long-term cost of a single tenured position can reach tens of millions of dollars, so schools allocate headcount as cautiously as an RTS caps population. The provost's most important decision is moving a faculty slot from one department to another; the department that loses it is sentenced to death, with talent draining away, while the winner gets a virtuous cycle. This is why CS explodes while the humanities shrink. Nuclear engineering is the counterexample: it was coveted in the 1970s, and for decades after Chernobyl schools kept paying salaries to an obsolete department.

points.h: Universities aren't temples of thought, they're outposts of federal industrial policy
points.body: Doing research at a university almost inevitably loses money, but it is the core of the American innovation system. Corporations long ago gave up on long-horizon research; universities are the only institutions willing to wait 20 years rather than for a financial return. The technology behind the COVID vaccines came from UPenn, PageRank and optogenetics from Stanford, open-source cryptography from MIT. The federal government reimburses research costs with tax dollars, universities publish for free, and private companies then productize it and sell it back to taxpayers at high prices. The government uses grants to steer universities toward national priorities — after the NIH budget doubled in the late 1990s, schools went on a frenzy of building towers and poaching people. So universities are not holy sites of independent thought but outposts of federal industrial policy, and cutting federal funding would instantly destroy the entire business model.

points.h: Harvard has the most money, but twelve schools keep it from moving
points.body: Princeton takes the narrow route: no medical school, no law school, no business school, entering biomedicine through quantitative theory, with research spending only one-fifth of Harvard's, yet it is not outmatched in any field. Its buildings were almost entirely donated by alumni, such as the $100 million energy center and the $180 million neuroscience institute. MIT is the opposite, so flush that it spent $400 million building a nanofabrication facility first and sold the naming rights afterward, filling new buildings with its own Nobel laureates, and in 2025 spun federally funded fusion research into a for-profit company. Harvard, by contrast, has twelve schools each controlling its own budget and endowment, and the money legally cannot be moved across them; its $1.4 billion cross-river campus stalled for six years during the financial crisis. The decentralized structure makes Harvard's strategy advance extremely slowly.

points.h: Challengers can't afford total war, so they bet on a single discipline
points.body: The top brand sits above all departments; the moment a new track appears, stars, donors, and applicants rush to Harvard and Stanford on day one. Lower-ranked schools cannot afford total war and can only bet on a single field to buy reputation: Babson bets on entrepreneurship, Johns Hopkins on medicine, Carnegie Mellon on CS and robotics, NYU on Stern and Tisch. Meanwhile, undergraduate scarcity is the fuel of the brand, and the admissions office's only goal is to maintain the scarcity of "you can't get in," with admissions officers guarding an empty counter like a Hermès salesperson. Early Decision forces students to commit to enrolling, artificially inflating yield and letting the school win on "first-choice" rankings.

quotes.text: There is something absurd about charging people nearly half a million dollars in cash for a piece of paper and then asking them to donate out of gratitude for the 4-year experience they paid for.
Their job is to whine and dine each of these individuals into upping their donations to six and seven figures.

This is why no student ever really meets or interacts with the college president. They'll give an occasional speech or pen a letter, but all their time is dedicated to closing the whales rather than the unripe undergrads who are decades away from writing a check.
Yet the twist is that the most reliable donors are not the whales, but instead the students who could never have afforded to attend.
After fees and on net returns, nearly every school has underperformed a run-of-the-mill Vanguard index fund, and no one has lost out on more than Harvard.
Donor restrictions are binding contracts that are enforcable for centuries by the donor's heirs and state attorneys.
Every year at a lesser school is another year wasted, and by the end, you'll have lost decades idling when you could otherwise have been doing your best work.
